recap_session: Thu Jul 2 (last full cash session; bond market early close 2 pm ET; equity market closed Fri Jul 3 in observance of Independence Day)
headline: A sharply below-consensus June jobs report took September Fed-hike odds off the table, lifting gold and bonds while the Dow set a record — but a second straight day of semiconductor selling knocked the Nasdaq 0.8% lower into the long weekend.
stance: Holiday weekend gap risk is real: US equity and bond markets are closed today (Sat Jul 4) and were closed yesterday (Fri Jul 3, holiday observed); the first live session is Monday Jul 6 at 9:30 am ET, meaning three days of news will reprice simultaneously. The soft payroll print was broadly read as removing pressure on the Fed to hike in September, which is a short-term positive for rate-sensitive assets and gold. The key fault line heading into Monday is whether the chip/AI re-rating is a healthy pause or the start of a broader tech unwind — that distinction will determine whether the S&P can hold its ground or gives back some of its 9.6% first-half gain.

news.head: June NFP: 57K — big miss
news.body: The US economy added just 57,000 jobs in June, well below the 110–115K consensus, with prior months revised down a combined 74,000 — the leisure and hospitality sector shed 61,000 jobs, the clearest drag.

news.head: Unemployment dipped, but for the wrong reason
news.body: The jobless rate edged to 4.2% from 4.3%, yet the improvement was driven by workers leaving the labor force: participation fell 0.3 percentage point to 61.5%, the lowest since March 2021.

news.head: September hike effectively priced out
news.body: Following the jobs print, traders removed a September rate increase from their base case; futures now point to a potential hike no earlier than October, according to market pricing, while the probability of any 2026 hike dropped materially.

news.head: Dow record, Nasdaq stumbles
news.body: The 30-stock Dow rose 595 points to a record close of 52,900.07 on Jul 2, lifted by Apple (+4.8%), Visa, and Walmart; the Nasdaq dropped 0.8% as semiconductors fell for a second straight session — the SMH chip ETF lost 4.5%, KLA slid 11.5%, and Teradyne fell 13.6%.

news.head: Meta cloud pivot rattles AI hardware trade
news.body: Meta said it would launch a cloud business and sell excess computing infrastructure, raising questions about whether big-tech AI capex has peaked and pressuring chip-equipment names.

news.head: Fed Chair Warsh at ECB Sintra
news.body: Warsh spoke at the European Central Bank conference in Portugal, acknowledged moderating inflation expectations but gave no forward guidance on rate policy and reaffirmed commitment to price stability.

news.head: Gold near $4,200 on jobs data
news.body: Gold climbed toward $4,200/oz (prior cash close Jul 3: $4,187.30) after the weak payroll print cooled rate-hike bets; the dollar fell to a two-week low on the same catalyst, providing additional support.

implications: The payroll miss is a net positive for bonds and gold but a double-edged signal for equities: rate-hike fear recedes (good for valuations) but softer growth raises earnings-revision risk heading into Q2 reporting season.
The Dow's record and S&P's near-flat close on the same day the Nasdaq fell 0.8% is a textbook rotation signal — money is moving from high-multiple tech into value, financials, and consumer staples.

With the bond market also closed Friday (full close) and equities dark all weekend, Monday's open absorbs three full days of global news at once — expect wider-than-normal bid/ask spreads and an outsized opening move in either direction.

Positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left in Nasdaq 100 futures (at the 4th percentile of 3-year positioning, a contrarian floor) and almost no bullish bets left in Russell 2000 futures (2nd percentile, contrarian floor) — both with divergence between speculator and hedger positioning, which historically has preceded short-covering rallies. In commodities, speculators are extended long in Copper (95th percentile, a contrarian warning) even as copper is at an extreme 3-year high of $6.224/lb. High-yield bond positioning sits at the 89th percentile — speculators are heavily positioned long there, a contrarian warning for credit.

watch.head: Monday open gap
watch.body: The first post-holiday session (Mon Jul 6, 9:30 am ET) absorbs three days of accumulated news — watch whether early moves are confirmed by volume and sector breadth or fade quickly.

watch.head: Semiconductor stabilization
watch.body: After two straight sessions of heavy selling in chip names (SMH -4.5% on Jul 2 alone), watch whether the group finds a floor Monday or continues to drag the Nasdaq.

watch.head: Fed July 29 meeting
watch.body: With September now off the table, all eyes shift to the July 29 FOMC meeting — any data between now and then that re-accelerates inflation could rapidly reprice hike odds higher.

watch.head: Gold above $4,200
watch.body: Gold (prior cash close Jul 3: $4,187.30, 81st 3-yr percentile) climbed toward $4,200 overnight on the jobs miss — a clean break and hold above that level would be a new bullish leg.

watch.head: JPY at extreme
watch.body: USD/JPY at 161.34 (prior cash close Jul 3) is at the 97.9th percentile of its 3-year range — an extreme level that raises the risk of Bank of Japan intervention; a rapid yen strengthening would ripple through risk assets globally.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: 10-year Treasury yield (prior cash close Jul 2): 4.49%; 2-year yield: 4.14% — the yield curve (2s10s) is a positive 35 basis points, meaning longer-term bonds yield more than short-term, a modest 'normalization' signal after years of inversion.
Real interest rates (inflation-adjusted 10-year yield) sit at 2.26% — still meaningfully positive, which keeps borrowing expensive and competes with equities for investor capital.

The 10-year inflation breakeven (market's implied inflation forecast) is 2.23% — below the Fed's 3-year-old inflation problem, suggesting bond markets believe inflation will eventually return near target.

Term premium (the extra yield investors demand to lend long-term) is 68.4 basis points — elevated, meaning investors are charging the government more to lock up money for a decade, a sign of fiscal unease.

Fed funds rate held at 3.50–3.75% at the June 17 meeting; the real (inflation-adjusted) fed funds rate is barely positive at 0.21%, giving the Fed room to stay on hold without cutting — the June payroll miss reinforces that path.

Bank reserves are $2,967 billion and the Treasury's cash account (TGA) is $880 billion — plentiful system liquidity; overnight repo (RRP) usage has collapsed to $2.2 billion, confirming no short-term funding stress.
ISM Manufacturing at 53.3 (readings above 50 signal expansion) — the factory sector is growing, a modest counterweight to the soft jobs number.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left in 3-month SOFR (short-term rate) futures — at the 1st percentile of 3-year positioning with hedger/speculator divergence — a contrarian signal that the market may be pricing in too much rate-hike risk for the front end.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: S&P 500 prior cash close (Jul 2): 7,483.24 — essentially flat on the day despite the jobs miss; Nasdaq 100 prior cash close: 25,832.67, down 0.8%; Dow Jones prior cash close: 52,900.07, a new all-time record.

S&P 500 futures overnight range ~7,527–7,565 (OVERNIGHT/PRE-MARKET levels); Dow futures overnight range ~53,080–53,388 (OVERNIGHT/PRE-MARKET); NDX futures overnight ~29,526–29,951 (OVERNIGHT/PRE-MARKET) — all pointing to modest implied gains when markets reopen Monday.

66.9% of S&P 500 stocks trade above their 50-day moving average and 67.1% above their 200-day moving average (as of Jul 2) — a healthy but not extreme breadth reading, consistent with a broad rally rather than a narrow bubble.

The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX, the market's 'fear gauge') closed at 15.81 on Jul 3 — calm; speculator positioning on VIX futures is at the 12th percentile (almost no one is betting on more volatility, a contrarian warning if conditions shift).

SKEW index at 150 (Jul 2) — elevated; this measures demand for deep out-of-the-money put options (tail-risk insurance); a high reading means institutional investors are quietly paying up to protect against a sharp sudden drop even as headline volatility appears low.
The Cyclical Adjusted P/E ratio (CAPE) for the S&P 500 is 41.6 — well above historical averages; at this valuation, the market leaves little room for earnings disappointments.

The equity risk premium — the extra return stocks offer over risk-free bonds — is negative at -2.05%, meaning bonds currently yield MORE than stocks on a risk-adjusted basis; this is a structurally unfavorable backdrop for equities versus history.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left in Nasdaq 100 futures (4th percentile, extended short, with hedger/speculator divergence — a contrarian floor). Russell 2000 futures are similarly extended short (2nd percentile, contrarian floor). These two readings together suggest a significant amount of pessimism is already priced into small- and mid-cap and growth positioning — any positive catalyst could trigger a sharp short-covering move (shorts are heavy, squeeze risk is elevated).

single_name.note: Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) — the world's dominant chip foundry — triggered a fresh long setup (score 6/10): large off-exchange block buying (quiet institutional accumulation), a burst of unusual options buying, company insiders have been buying (1 insider rule fired), and the stock is trading above its long-term 200-day trend line. Shorts are relatively light (1.8 days to cover), limiting squeeze risk but also meaning the setup is driven by genuine buying rather than forced covering. Relevant given the semiconductor sell-off: if AI chip demand is truly intact, TSM is where it would show up first.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: High-yield corporate bond spreads (the extra interest rate junk-rated companies pay over Treasuries) are 275 basis points (Jul 2) — benign; wide spreads would signal corporate stress, and this level does not.
Investment-grade corporate bond spreads are 75 basis points (Jul 2) — also calm; blue-chip companies can borrow cheaply.

The FRA-OIS spread (a measure of short-term bank-to-bank lending stress — think of it as a 'financial plumbing' health check) is just 3 basis points — essentially zero stress; funding markets are operating normally.
The commercial paper funding spread (the cost for companies to borrow short-term cash) is 26 basis points — low, confirming no corporate liquidity crunch.
Bank credit growth is running at 6.33% year-over-year (as of Jun 24) — solid; banks are lending, which supports economic activity.
M2 money supply is growing 5.58% year-over-year — moderate; not inflationary-fast, but enough to support nominal growth.

The equity-credit correlation stands at 0.718 (Jul 2) — stocks and credit are moving together, which is typical in a 'risk-on' environment; a breakdown in this correlation would be an early warning sign.

single_name.note: Matador Resources (MTDR) — Energy sector — top-ranked setup (score 7/10): large off-exchange block buying (quiet institutional accumulation), a burst of unusual options buying, 2 insider rules fired (company insiders have been buying), trading above its 200-day trend line. Shorts are heavy at 7.64 days to cover — meaningful squeeze risk if oil stabilizes. Crude oil (prior cash close Jul 3: $68.78/bbl) is at the 35th percentile of its 3-year range — calm but with room to recover, which would directly benefit Matador's E&P revenue.
